بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ

Makkiyyah (revealed in Makkah). It has eighty-nine verses, eight hundred and thirty-three words, and three thousand four hundred letters.

Ibn al-Muqri told us: Ibn Mattar told us: Ibn Shurayk told us: Ibn Yunus told us: Sallam ibn Sulaym told us: Harun ibn Kathir told us, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father, from Abu Umamah al-Bahili, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Surat al-Zukhruf will be among those who are told on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿O My servants, no fear shall be upon you this Day, nor shall you grieve. Enter Paradise without reckoning.﴾" [191] [Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan (Majma' al-Bayan li-'Ulum al-Qur'an): 9/66].

Allah the Exalted said:

﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.﴾

﴿Ha Mim. By the Manifest Book, indeed We have made it an Arabic Qur'an.﴾ That is, We sent it down, named it, explained it, and described it.

This is like His saying: ﴿Allah did not institute any bahirah or sa'ibah﴾ [Surat al-Ma'idah: 103], and His saying: ﴿And they made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾ [Surat al-Zukhruf: 19], and His saying: ﴿They made the Qur'an into parts﴾ [Surat al-Hijr: 91], and His saying: ﴿Do you consider the giving of drink to the pilgrims...﴾ [Surat al-Tawbah: 19]. All of these carry the meaning of description and naming, and it is impossible that they mean creation.

﴿That you may understand.﴾ ﴿And indeed it is in the Mother of the Book﴾ means this Book. ﴿With Us, it is exalted and wise.﴾ The "Mother of the Book" means the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), which is with Allah, and from which [revelation] is copied (yunsakh). Qatadah said: it is the origin of the Book and its entirety.

Abdullah ibn Hamid al-Wazzan told us: Makki ibn Iydan told us: Abdullah ibn Hashim ibn Hayyan told us: Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Qattan told us: Hisham al-Dastawa'i told us: al-Qasim ibn Abi Yazzah told me: 'Urwah ibn 'Amir al-Qurashi told me, who said: I heard Ibn 'Abbas say: "The first thing Allah the Exalted created was the pen, and He commanded it to write what He wished to create, and the Book was with Him." Then he recited: ﴿And indeed it is in the Mother of the Book with Us, exalted and wise. Shall We then withhold the Reminder from you, turning away from you, because you are a transgressing people?﴾

Scholars differed about its meaning. A group said: "Shall We withhold the punishment and hold back, turn away from you, and leave you, so that We do not punish you for your disbelief." This is the view of Mujahid, al-Suddi, and a narration of al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Do you think He will overlook you while you have not understood what you were commanded?" Others said: its meaning is, "Shall We withhold sending down the Qur'an and abandon it because you do not believe in it, so We do not send it down and do not repeat it to you." This is the view of Qatadah and Ibn Zayd.

Qatadah said: "By Allah, if this Qur'an had been lifted when the first of this nation rejected it, they would have perished. But Allah, out of His kindness and mercy, returned to them, repeated it to them, and called them to it for twenty years, or whatever Allah willed of that."

al-Kalbi said: "Shall We leave you neglected, not commanding you and not forbidding you?" al-Kisa'i said: "Shall We roll up the Reminder from you, so that you are not called and not admonished?"

This is among the eloquent expressions of the Qur'an. The Arabs say of one who refrains from something and turns away from it: "Daraba 'anhu safhan" (he struck it aside with the side), and the origin of this is that when you turn away from someone, you turn the side of your neck toward him. Kuthayyir said:

*"Turning away; you meet me only with a grudging face,*
*So whoever tires of that, the union tires [too]."*

That is, turning her face away. And "darabtu 'an kadha" or "adrabtu" means that when you leave something and refrain from it.

﴿An kuntum﴾: the people of Madinah and Kufah, except 'Asim, read the alif of ﴿an﴾ as written with the meaning of ﴿idh﴾ ("when"), like His saying: ﴿And leave what remains of usury, if you are believers﴾ [Surat al-Baqarah: 278], and His saying: ﴿If they desire chastity﴾ [Surat al-Nur: 33].

The others read it with a fatha, meaning "because you were," with the sense of past tense, as one says in speech: "I curse you if you deprived me," meaning "when you deprived me." Abu 'Ubaydah said: "The accusative reading is more beloved to me, because Allah reproached them for what they had done, and He had known their deed beforehand."

﴿A people who are extravagant﴾ means polytheists who exceed the command of Allah.

﴿And how many a prophet We sent among the earlier peoples, but no prophet came to them﴾ means: and no prophet used to come to them, ﴿except that they mocked him﴾, like the mockery of your people toward you. This consoles His Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿So We destroyed those who were stronger than them in might﴾, meaning in strength. ﴿And the example of the earlier peoples has passed﴾ means their condition, their practice, and their punishment.

﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "They were created by the Almighty, the All-Knowing, who made the earth for you as a cradle and made for you therein roads, that you may be guided. And who sends down water from the sky in measure﴾, that is, in the amount of your need for it. ﴿And We revive thereby a dead land﴾, that is, We gave life. ﴿Thus you will be brought forth﴾ from your graves alive, just as We revived this dead land with rain.

﴿And who created all the pairs﴾, meaning the kinds. ﴿And made for you ships and cattle on which you ride, that you may sit firmly upon their backs﴾. The pronoun is singular because it refers back to ﴿ma﴾. al-Farra' said: He attributed the back (zuhur) to the singular because that singular has the meaning of a plural, like "jund" (army), "jaysh" (host), "rahT" (group), "khayl" (horses), and similar collective nouns for armies.

﴿Then you remember the favor of your Lord when you are seated upon them, and say, "Glory be to Him who has subjected these to us, and we were not capable of that."﴾ That is, we were not able to control and subdue them. This is from the Qur'an, as if it intended: "We were not able to overcome it in strength."

﴿And indeed, to our Lord we are returning﴾, meaning we will be returned in the Hereafter.

Ibn Fanjawayh al-Dinawari told us: Sa'id ibn Muhammad ibn Ishaq al-Sayrafi told us: Muhammad ibn 'Uthman ibn Abi Shaybah told us: Muhammad ibn 'Imran ibn Abi Layla told us: my father told us, from Ibn Abi Layla, from al-Hakam, from 'Ali ibn Rabi'ah, from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), that when he placed his foot in the stirrup he would say, "In the name of Allah," and when he was seated upon the mount he would say, "Praise be to Allah for every state. ﴿Glory be to Him who has subjected these to us, and we were not capable of that. And indeed, to our Lord we are returning.﴾" Then he would say "Allahu akbar" three times and "La ilaha illa Allah" three times. [192] [Kitab al-Du'a (Kitab al-Du'a) of al-Tabarani: 248].

Qatadah said: In this verse He teaches you what to say when you ride in ships and cattle; you say: ﴿And say, "My Lord, cause me to land at a blessed landing place, and You are the best of those who bring to land."﴾ [Surat al-Mu'minun: 29].

﴿And they have made for Him from His servants a portion﴾, meaning these polytheists. That is, a share and a part.

Mujahid and Qatadah said: "'Idl," meaning an equal, and that is their saying that the angels are the daughters of Allah the Exalted.

﴿Indeed, mankind is clearly ungrateful.﴾

This is like His saying: ﴿Allah did not institute any bahirah or sa'ibah﴾ [Surat al-Ma'idah: 103], and His saying: ﴿And they made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾ [Surat al-Zukhruf: 19], and His saying: ﴿They made the Qur'an into parts﴾ [Surat al-Hijr: 91], and His saying: ﴿Do you consider the giving of drink to the pilgrims...﴾ [Surat al-Tawbah: 19]. All of these carry the meaning of description and naming, and it is impossible that they mean creation.

﴿That you may understand.﴾ ﴿And indeed it is in the Mother of the Book﴾ means this Book. ﴿With Us, it is exalted and wise.﴾ The "Mother of the Book" means the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), which is with Allah, and from which [revelation] is copied (yunsakh). Qatadah said: it is the origin of the Book and its entirety.

Abdullah ibn Hamid al-Wazzan told us: Makki ibn Iydan told us: Abdullah ibn Hashim ibn Hayyan told us: Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Qattan told us: Hisham al-Dastawa'i told us: al-Qasim ibn Abi Yazzah told me: 'Urwah ibn 'Amir al-Qurashi told me, who said: I heard Ibn 'Abbas say: "The first thing Allah the Exalted created was the pen, and He commanded it to write what He wished to create, and the Book was with Him." Then he recited: ﴿And indeed it is in the Mother of the Book with Us, exalted and wise. Shall We then withhold the Reminder from you, turning away from you, because you are a transgressing people?﴾

Scholars differed about its meaning. A group said: "Shall We withhold the punishment and hold back, turn away from you, and leave you, so that We do not punish you for your disbelief." This is the view of Mujahid, al-Suddi, and a narration of al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Do you think He will overlook you while you have not understood what you were commanded?" Others said: its meaning is, "Shall We withhold sending down the Qur'an and abandon it because you do not believe in it, so We do not send it down and do not repeat it to you." This is the view of Qatadah and Ibn Zayd.

Qatadah said: "By Allah, if this Qur'an had been lifted when the first of this nation rejected it, they would have perished. But Allah, out of His kindness and mercy, returned to them, repeated it to them, and called them to it for twenty years, or whatever Allah willed of that."

al-Kalbi said: "Shall We leave you neglected, not commanding you and not forbidding you?" al-Kisa'i said: "Shall We roll up the Reminder from you, so that you are not called and not admonished?"

This is among the eloquent expressions of the Qur'an. The Arabs say of one who refrains from something and turns away from it: "Daraba 'anhu safhan" (he struck it aside with the side), and the origin of this is that when you turn away from someone, you turn the side of your neck toward him. Kuthayyir said:

*"Turning away; you meet me only with a grudging face,*
*So whoever tires of that, the union tires [too]."*

That is, turning her face away. And "darabtu 'an kadha" or "adrabtu" means that when you leave something and refrain from it.

﴿An kuntum﴾: the people of Madinah and Kufah, except 'Asim, read the alif of ﴿an﴾ as written with the meaning of ﴿idh﴾ ("when"), like His saying: ﴿And leave what remains of usury, if you are believers﴾ [Surat al-Baqarah: 278], and His saying: ﴿If they desire chastity﴾ [Surat al-Nur: 33].

The others read it with a fatha, meaning "because you were," with the sense of past tense, as one says in speech: "I curse you if you deprived me," meaning "when you deprived me." Abu 'Ubaydah said: "The accusative reading is more beloved to me, because Allah reproached them for what they had done, and He had known their deed beforehand."

﴿A people who are extravagant﴾ means polytheists who exceed the command of Allah.

﴿And how many a prophet We sent among the earlier peoples, but no prophet came to them﴾ means: and no prophet used to come to them, ﴿except that they mocked him﴾, like the mockery of your people toward you. This consoles His Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿So We destroyed those who were stronger than them in might﴾, meaning in strength. ﴿And the example of the earlier peoples has passed﴾ means their condition, their practice, and their punishment.

﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "They were created by the Almighty, the All-Knowing, who made the earth for you as a cradle and made for you therein roads, that you may be guided. And who sends down water from the sky in measure﴾, that is, in the amount of your need for it. ﴿And We revive thereby a dead land﴾, that is, We gave life. ﴿Thus you will be brought forth﴾ from your graves alive, just as We revived this dead land with rain.

﴿And who created all the pairs﴾, meaning the kinds. ﴿And made for you ships and cattle on which you ride, that you may sit firmly upon their backs﴾. The pronoun is singular because it refers back to ﴿ma﴾. al-Farra' said: He attributed the back (zuhur) to the singular because that singular has the meaning of a plural, like "jund" (army), "jaysh" (host), "rahT" (group), "khayl" (horses), and similar collective nouns for armies.

﴿Then you remember the favor of your Lord when you are seated upon them, and say, "Glory be to Him who has subjected these to us, and we were not capable of that."﴾ That is, we were not able to control and subdue them. This is from the Qur'an, as if it intended: "We were not able to overcome it in strength."

﴿And indeed, to our Lord we are returning﴾, meaning we will be returned in the Hereafter.

Ibn Fanjawayh al-Dinawari told us: Sa'id ibn Muhammad ibn Ishaq al-Sayrafi told us: Muhammad ibn 'Uthman ibn Abi Shaybah told us: Muhammad ibn 'Imran ibn Abi Layla told us: my father told us, from Ibn Abi Layla, from al-Hakam, from 'Ali ibn Rabi'ah, from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), that when he placed his foot in the stirrup he would say, "In the name of Allah," and when he was seated upon the mount he would say, "Praise be to Allah for every state. ﴿Glory be to Him who has subjected these to us, and we were not capable of that. And indeed, to our Lord we are returning.﴾" Then he would say "Allahu akbar" three times and "La ilaha illa Allah" three times. [192] [Kitab al-Du'a (Kitab al-Du'a) of al-Tabarani: 248].

Qatadah said: In this verse He teaches you what to say when you ride in ships and cattle; you say: ﴿And say, "My Lord, cause me to land at a blessed landing place, and You are the best of those who bring to land."﴾ [Surat al-Mu'minun: 29].

﴿And they have made for Him from His servants a portion﴾, meaning these polytheists. That is, a share and a part.

Mujahid and Qatadah said: "'Idl," meaning an equal, and that is their saying that the angels are the daughters of Allah the Exalted.

﴿Indeed, mankind is clearly ungrateful.﴾

بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ

Makkiyyah (revealed in Makkah). It has eighty-nine verses, eight hundred and thirty-three words, and three thousand four hundred letters.

Ibn al-Muqri told us: Ibn Mattar told us: Ibn Shurayk told us: Ibn Yunus told us: Sallam ibn Sulaym told us: Harun ibn Kathir told us, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father, from Abu Umamah al-Bahili, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Surat al-Zukhruf will be among those who are told on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿O My servants, no fear shall be upon you this Day, nor shall you grieve. Enter Paradise without reckoning.﴾" [191] [Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan (Majma' al-Bayan li-'Ulum al-Qur'an): 9/66].

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 43, verses 16–35:**

﴿Or has He taken daughters from what He creates, and chosen sons for you?﴾ *Akhlasakum* (chosen you), *wa-khassasakum* (singled you out) with sons. Its parallel is His saying, ﴿Has your Lord then chosen sons for you and taken daughters from the angels?﴾ [[Surah al-Isra': 40.]]

﴿And when one of them is given good news of that which he attributes to the Most Merciful, his face becomes darkened, and he is filled with suppressed grief﴾: meaning daughters. Its evidence is in al-Nahl: ﴿his face becomes darkened, and he is filled with suppressed grief﴾, from sorrow and rage.

﴿Or one who is brought up in ornaments﴾: the people of Kufa read *yunashsha'u* with a *damma* on the *ya'*, a *fatha* on the *nun*, and a *shadda* on the *shin*, in the passive voice, meaning "one who is raised by others." Others read *yanshu'u* with a *fatha* on the *ya'*, a *jazm* on the *nun*, and a lightened *shin*, meaning "grows up and becomes great."

﴿In the ornament﴾: in adornment, meaning women. Mujahid said: He permitted women silk and gold, and he recited this verse.

Abdullah ibn Hamid informed us: Muhammad ibn al-Husayn al-Za'farani informed us: Yahya ibn Ja'far ibn Abi Talib related to us: Muhammad ibn Ubayd related to us: Ubaydullah ibn Umar related to us, from Nafi', from Sa'id ibn Abi Hind, from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Gold and silk are forbidden to the males of my community and lawful to its females" [193] [[Fath al-Bari: 10/250; Muntakhab Musnad 'Abd ibn Humayd: 193.]].

﴿And he is not clear in dispute﴾: lacking clarity of argument, due to their weakness and foolishness. Qatada said regarding this verse: A woman seldom speaks with her argument without the argument turning against her. In the Codex of Abdullah (*wa-huwa fi al-kalam ghayr mubin*) [and he is not clear in speech].

Some exegetes said: This verse refers to their idols which they worshipped, honored, and adorned, though they do not speak or utter a sound. Ibn Zayd said: These are their images which they make of silver and gold, and they adorn them and worship them.

*Man* in *Awa-man yunashsha'u* has three possible grammatical positions (*wujuh*): the nominative (*raf'*) as the subject of a new sentence (*ibtida'*); the accusative (*nasb*) by an implied verb, whose sense is: "they make it a lord or daughters of Allah"; and the genitive (*khafd*), in response to His saying *mimma yakhluqu* [from what He creates] and His saying: *bima sarat* [by what they have become]...

﴿And they have made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾: Abu 'Amr and the people of Kufa read *'ibad al-Rahman* with an alif and a *ya'*, and Abu 'Ubayd chose this reading, saying: Because the attribution in it is higher, and because Allah only denied them in His saying "daughters of Allah," so He informed that they are His servants and not His daughters. This is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas.

Muhammad ibn Na'im informed us: al-Husayn ibn Ayyub informed us: 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-Aziz informed us: al-Qasim ibn Salam informed us: Haytham related to us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he read it *'Ibadu al-Rahman*.

Sa'id said: I said to Ibn 'Abbas: "In my codex it is *'Abd al-Rahman*." He said: "Erase it and write *'Ibad al-Rahman*." The confirmation of this reading is His saying: ﴿Rather, they are honored servants﴾ [[Surah al-Anbiya': 26.]]. The others read *'inda al-Rahman* with a *nun*, and Abu Hatim chose this, saying: Because this is praise, whereas when you say *'Ibad al-Rahman* [servants of the Most Merciful], its confirmation is His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord﴾ [[Surah al-A'raf: 206.]].

﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾: did they attend their creation, so that they would know that they are females? The people of Medina read *ushhidu* in the passive voice, meaning "were they made to witness." *Khalqahum*: at the time they were created. ﴿Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned﴾: that the angels are daughters of Allah.

﴿And they say: "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them"﴾: meaning the angels, according to Qatada, Muqatil, and al-Kalbi. Mujahid said: it means the idols. They said that Allah did not hasten punishment upon them for worshipping them, which indicates His approval of their worship. Allah said: ﴿They have no knowledge of that. They are only guessing﴾, meaning lying.

﴿Or have We given them a Book before this, so they are holding fast to it?﴾: that is, before this Qur'an. ﴿Rather, they say: "We found our fathers upon a religion (*ummah*)", and we are guided by their footsteps.﴾ The common reading is *ummatin* with a *damma* on the *alif*, meaning religion and creed. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Aziz and Mujahid read *'immatin* with a *kasra* on the *alif*, and they differed on its meaning. It was said it means the path and the aim, from their saying *amamtu* [I aimed]. It was said it means blessing. 'Adi ibn Zayd said: "After prosperity, dominion, and blessing (*al-umma*), and We showed them the graves there." It was also said that the two are dialects with one meaning.

﴿And similarly, We did not send before you a warner to a town except that its affluent ones said: "We found our fathers upon a religion, and we are following in their footsteps."﴾: *mustanun* (following), *muttabi'un* (adhering).

*Qal* [he said]: the common reading is in the imperative. Ibn 'Amir read it in the declarative, and Hafs ibn 'Asim related the same.

﴿"Even if I brought you better guidance than that which you found your fathers upon?"﴾: Abu Ja'far read *awa-law ja'akum* with an *alif* [as a question]. The rest read *ji'tukum* in the singular. *Bi-ahda*: with a more correct religion. ﴿They said: "Indeed, we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent." So We took retribution upon them. Then observe how was the end of the deniers.﴾

﴿And [mention] when Abraham said to his father and his people: "Indeed, I am free (*bara'*) from what you worship"﴾: *bara'* means "free"; it is not dualized, pluralized, or feminized, because it is a verbal noun placed in the position of an adjective. In the reading of Abdullah it is *bari'*, with a *ya'*. ﴿Except for He who created me, for He will guide me﴾: created me; the meaning of the verse is: "I am free from every deity except He who created me, for He will guide me to His religion."

﴿And He made it (*wa-ja'alaha*), referring to this statement and word, a word that remains among his descendants﴾: Mujahid and Qatada said: it means *la ilaha illa Allah* [there is no god but Allah]. Al-Qurazi said: it means the will of Abraham that he enjoined upon his sons, which remains in his progeny and offspring, and which Allah mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿And Abraham instructed his sons with it﴾ [[Surah al-Baqarah: 132.]]. Ibn Zayd said: it means his saying: ﴿I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [[Surah al-Baqarah: 131.]], and he recited ﴿He named you "the Muslims"﴾ [[Surah al-Hajj: 78.]].

﴿So that they may return﴾ from their disbelief to obedience, and repent. ﴿But I gave enjoyment to these and their fathers﴾ in this world, so I did not destroy them, nor hasten punishment upon them for their disbelief. ﴿Until there came to them the truth﴾: the Qur'an. Al-Dahhak said: Islam. ﴿And a clear messenger﴾: who clarifies for them the signs and the rulings, and he is Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿And when the truth came to them, the Qur'an, they said: "This is magic, and we disbelieve in it."﴾ ﴿And they said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two towns?"﴾ That is, from one of the two towns. They did not differ that the two towns are Mecca and al-Ta'if, but they differed about who the two men were. Ibn 'Abbas said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira from Mecca, who was called the "basil of Quraysh," and Habib ibn 'Amr ibn 'Umayr al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if.

Mujahid said: 'Utba ibn al-Rabi'a from Mecca, and Ibn 'Abd Yalil al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if. Qatada said: they are al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi and Abu Mas'ud 'Urwa ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi. Al-Suddi said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and Kinana ibn 'Abd 'Amr ibn 'Umayr.

Allah the Glorified and Exalted said: ﴿Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord?﴾: His prophethood and honor, so that they would give it to whomever they wish. ﴿We have distributed among them their livelihood in the life of this world﴾: We made this one rich and that one poor, this one a king and that one a subject. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Yahya read *ma'ayishahum* [their livelihoods]. ﴿And We raised some of them above others in degrees, that some of them may take others in service (*sukhriyyan*)﴾: that the wealthy may employ the poor laborers with their wealth through work, and that they may use them, so that some become a means of livelihood for others in this world: this one with his wealth, and that one with his work. This is the saying of al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. Qatada and al-Dahhak said: meaning that some own others, so this one is the slave of that one. It was said: some mock others. It was said: some subjugate others.

﴿And the mercy of your Lord﴾: meaning Paradise, ﴿is better than what they accumulate﴾ of wealth in this world. ﴿And if not that the people would become one community﴾: united in disbelief, so they would all become disbelievers. This is the saying of most exegetes. Ibn Zayd said: meaning: ﴿and if not that the people would become one community﴾ in pursuit of the world and preferring it over the Hereafter.

﴿We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful, for their houses, roofs of silver﴾: Abu Ja'far, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Humayd, and Yahya ibn Wathhab read *saqfan* with a *fatha* on the *sin*, in the singular, meaning the plural, by analogy with His saying: ﴿So the roof fell upon them from above them﴾ [[Surah al-Nahl: 26.]]. The rest read *suqufan* with a *damma* on the *sin* and *qaf*, in the plural. It is said *saqf* and *saqqaf*, like *rahn* and *rahhan*. Abu 'Ubayd said: there is no third reading for them. It was said it is the plural of *saqif*, and it was said it is the plural of *suqf*, and the plural of the plural. ﴿And stairways﴾: that is, ascents, steps, and ladders. Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi read *ma'arij*, and both are dialects; the singular is *mi'raj*, like *maftah* and *mafatih*.

﴿Upon which they would ascend﴾: rise up, climb, and ascend by them. One says *zahartu 'ala al-sath* [I ascended upon the roof] when you climb it. Al-Nabigha al-Ja'di said:

"Our glory and splendor have reached the heavens, and we hope for a height beyond that."

That is, an ascent.

﴿And for their houses, doors of silver, and couches of silver upon which they recline, and ornamentation﴾: meaning, We would also have given them, besides that, ornamentation, which is gold, like the phrase "a decorated house." It may be that the meaning is "silver and ornamentation," and when the preposition is removed it becomes accusative.

﴿And all that is but the enjoyment of the life of this world﴾: Asim and Hamza read *lamma* with a *shadda* on the *mim* [meaning "all of it" as an emphatic], as in *wa-in kullu dhalika lamma mata'u al-hayat al-dunya*. Some exegetes said: This verse refers to their idols which they worshipped, honored, and adorned, though they do not speak or utter a sound. Ibn Zayd said: These are their images which they make of silver and gold, and they adorn them and worship them.

Muhammad ibn Na'im informed us: al-Husayn ibn Ayyub informed us: 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-Aziz informed us: al-Qasim ibn Salam informed us: Haytham related to us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he read it *'Ibadu al-Rahman*.

Sa'id said: I said to Ibn 'Abbas: "In my codex it is *'Abd al-Rahman*." He said: "Erase it and write *'Ibad al-Rahman*." The confirmation of this reading is His saying: ﴿Rather, they are honored servants﴾ [[Surah al-Anbiya': 26.]]. The others read *'inda al-Rahman* with a *nun*, and Abu Hatim chose this, saying: Because this is praise, whereas when you say *'Ibad al-Rahman* [servants of the Most Merciful], its confirmation is His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord﴾ [[Surah al-A'raf: 206.]].

﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾: did they attend their creation, so that they would know that they are females? *Qal* [he said]: the common reading is in the imperative. Ibn 'Amir read it in the declarative, and Hafs ibn 'Asim related the same.

﴿"Even if I brought you better guidance than that which you found your fathers upon?"﴾: Abu Ja'far read *awa-law ja'akum* with an *alif* [as a question]. The rest read *ji'tukum* in the singular. *Bi-ahda*: with a more correct religion. ﴿They said: "Indeed, we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent." So We took retribution upon them. Then observe how was the end of the deniers.﴾

﴿And [mention] when Abraham said to his father and his people: "Indeed, I am free (*bara'*) from what you worship"﴾: *bara'* means "free"; it is not dualized, pluralized, or feminized, because it is a verbal noun placed in the position of an adjective. In the reading of Abdullah it is *bari'*, with a *ya'*. ﴿Except for He who created me, for He will guide me﴾: created me; the meaning of the verse is: "I am free from every deity except He who created me, for He will guide me to His religion."

Al-Qurazi said: it means the will of Abraham that he enjoined upon his sons, which remains in his progeny and offspring, and which Allah mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿And Abraham instructed his sons with it﴾ [[Surah al-Baqarah: 132.]]. ﴿So that they may return﴾ from their disbelief to obedience, and repent. ﴿But I gave enjoyment to these and their fathers﴾ in this world, so I did not destroy them, nor hasten punishment upon them for their disbelief. ﴿Until there came to them the truth﴾: the Qur'an. Al-Dahhak said: Islam. ﴿And a clear messenger﴾: who clarifies for them the signs and the rulings, and he is Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿And when the truth came to them, the Qur'an, they said: "This is magic, and we disbelieve in it."﴾ ﴿And they said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two towns?"﴾ That is, from one of the two towns. Ibn 'Abbas said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira from Mecca, who was called the "basil of Quraysh," and Habib ibn 'Amr ibn 'Umayr al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if.

Mujahid said: 'Utba ibn al-Rabi'a from Mecca, and Ibn 'Abd Yalil al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if. Qatada said: they are al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi and Abu Mas'ud 'Urwa ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi. Al-Suddi said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and Kinana ibn 'Abd 'Amr ibn 'Umayr.

Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Yahya read *ma'ayishahum* [their livelihoods]. ﴿And We raised some of them above others in degrees, that some of them may take others in service (*sukhriyyan*)﴾: that the wealthy may employ the poor laborers with their wealth through work, and that they may use them, so that some become a means of livelihood for others in this world: this one with his wealth, and that one with his work. It was said: some subjugate others.

Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi read *ma'arij*, and both are dialects; the singular is *mi'raj*, like *maftah* and *mafatih*.

"Our glory and splendor have reached the heavens, and we hope for a height beyond that."

That is, an ascent.

﴿And for their houses, doors of silver, and couches of silver upon which they recline, and ornamentation﴾: meaning, We would also have given them, besides that, ornamentation, which is gold, like the phrase "a decorated house." It may be that the meaning is "silver and ornamentation," and when the preposition is removed it becomes accusative.

﴿Or one who is brought up in ornaments﴾: the people of Kufa read *yunashsha'u* with a *damma* on the *ya'*, a *fatha* on the *nun*, and a *shadda* on the *shin*, in the passive voice, meaning "one who is raised by others." Others read *yanshu'u* with a *fatha* on the *ya'*, a *jazm* on the *nun*, and a lightened *shin*, meaning "grows up and becomes great."

﴿In the ornament﴾: in adornment, meaning women. Mujahid said: He permitted women silk and gold, and he recited this verse.

Abdullah ibn Hamid informed us: Muhammad ibn al-Husayn al-Za'farani informed us: Yahya ibn Ja'far ibn Abi Talib related to us: Muhammad ibn Ubayd related to us: Ubaydullah ibn Umar related to us, from Nafi', from Sa'id ibn Abi Hind, from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Gold and silk are forbidden to the males of my community and lawful to its females" [193] [[Fath al-Bari: 10/250; Muntakhab Musnad 'Abd ibn Humayd: 193.]].

﴿And he is not clear in dispute﴾: lacking clarity of argument, due to their weakness and foolishness. Qatada said regarding this verse: A woman seldom speaks with her argument without the argument turning against her. In the Codex of Abdullah (*wa-huwa fi al-kalam ghayr mubin*) [and he is not clear in speech].

Some exegetes said: This verse refers to their idols which they worshipped, honored, and adorned, though they do not speak or utter a sound. Ibn Zayd said: These are their images which they make of silver and gold, and they adorn them and worship them.

This is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas.

Muhammad ibn Na'im informed us: al-Husayn ibn Ayyub informed us: 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-Aziz informed us: al-Qasim ibn Salam informed us: Haytham related to us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he read it *'Ibadu al-Rahman*.

Sa'id said: I said to Ibn 'Abbas: "In my codex it is *'Abd al-Rahman*." He said: "Erase it and write *'Ibad al-Rahman*." The confirmation of this reading is His saying: ﴿Rather, they are honored servants﴾ [[Surah al-Anbiya': 26.]]. The others read *'inda al-Rahman* with a *nun*, and Abu Hatim chose this, saying: Because this is praise, whereas when you say *'Ibad al-Rahman* [servants of the Most Merciful], its confirmation is His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord﴾ [[Surah al-A'raf: 206.]].

﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾: did they attend their creation, so that they would know that they are females? The people of Medina read *ushhidu* in the passive voice, meaning "were they made to witness." *Khalqahum*: at the time they were created. ﴿Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned﴾: that the angels are daughters of Allah.

﴿And they say: "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them"﴾: meaning the angels, according to Qatada, Muqatil, and al-Kalbi. Mujahid said: it means the idols. They are only guessing﴾, meaning lying.

It was said it means blessing. 'Adi ibn Zayd said: "After prosperity, dominion, and blessing (*al-umma*), and We showed them the graves there." It was also said that the two are dialects with one meaning.

*Qal* [he said]: the common reading is in the imperative. Ibn 'Amir read it in the declarative, and Hafs ibn 'Asim related the same.

﴿"Even if I brought you better guidance than that which you found your fathers upon?"﴾: Abu Ja'far read *awa-law ja'akum* with an *alif* [as a question]. The rest read *ji'tukum* in the singular. *Bi-ahda*: with a more correct religion. ﴿They said: "Indeed, we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent." So We took retribution upon them. Then observe how was the end of the deniers.﴾

﴿And [mention] when Abraham said to his father and his people: "Indeed, I am free (*bara'*) from what you worship"﴾: *bara'* means "free"; it is not dualized, pluralized, or feminized, because it is a verbal noun placed in the position of an adjective. In the reading of Abdullah it is *bari'*, with a *ya'*. ﴿Except for He who created me, for He will guide me﴾: created me; the meaning of the verse is: "I am free from every deity except He who created me, for He will guide me to His religion."

﴿And He made it (*wa-ja'alaha*), referring to this statement and word, a word that remains among his descendants﴾: Mujahid and Qatada said: it means *la ilaha illa Allah* [there is no god but Allah]. Al-Qurazi said: it means the will of Abraham that he enjoined upon his sons, which remains in his progeny and offspring, and which Allah mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿And Abraham instructed his sons with it﴾ [[Surah al-Baqarah: 132.]]. Ibn Zayd said: it means his saying: ﴿I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [[Surah al-Baqarah: 131.]], and he recited ﴿He named you "the Muslims"﴾ [[Surah al-Hajj: 78.]].

﴿So that they may return﴾ from their disbelief to obedience, and repent. ﴿But I gave enjoyment to these and their fathers﴾ in this world, so I did not destroy them, nor hasten punishment upon them for their disbelief. ﴿Until there came to them the truth﴾: the Qur'an. Al-Dahhak said: Islam. ﴿And a clear messenger﴾: who clarifies for them the signs and the rulings, and he is Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿And when the truth came to them, the Qur'an, they said: "This is magic, and we disbelieve in it."﴾ ﴿And they said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two towns?"﴾ That is, from one of the two towns. They did not differ that the two towns are Mecca and al-Ta'if, but they differed about who the two men were. Ibn 'Abbas said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira from Mecca, who was called the "basil of Quraysh," and Habib ibn 'Amr ibn 'Umayr al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if.

Mujahid said: 'Utba ibn al-Rabi'a from Mecca, and Ibn 'Abd Yalil al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if. Qatada said: they are al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi and Abu Mas'ud 'Urwa ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi. Al-Suddi said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and Kinana ibn 'Abd 'Amr ibn 'Umayr.

Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Yahya read *ma'ayishahum* [their livelihoods]. ﴿And We raised some of them above others in degrees, that some of them may take others in service (*sukhriyyan*)﴾: that the wealthy may employ the poor laborers with their wealth through work, and that they may use them, so that some become a means of livelihood for others in this world: this one with his wealth, and that one with his work. This is the saying of al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. Qatada and al-Dahhak said: meaning that some own others, so this one is the slave of that one. It was said: some mock others. It was said: some subjugate others.

﴿And the mercy of your Lord﴾: meaning Paradise, ﴿is better than what they accumulate﴾ of wealth in this world. ﴿And if not that the people would become one community﴾: united in disbelief, so they would all become disbelievers. This is the saying of most exegetes. Ibn Zayd said: meaning: ﴿and if not that the people would become one community﴾ in pursuit of the world and preferring it over the Hereafter.

﴿We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful, for their houses, roofs of silver﴾: Abu Ja'far, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Humayd, and Yahya ibn Wathhab read *saqfan* with a *fatha* on the *sin*, in the singular, meaning the plural, by analogy with His saying: ﴿So the roof fell upon them from above them﴾ [[Surah al-Nahl: 26.]]. Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi read *ma'arij*, and both are dialects; the singular is *mi'raj*, like *maftah* and *mafatih*.

"Our glory and splendor have reached the heavens, and we hope for a height beyond that."

That is, an ascent.

﴿And for their houses, doors of silver, and couches of silver upon which they recline, and ornamentation﴾: meaning, We would also have given them, besides that, ornamentation, which is gold, like the phrase "a decorated house." It may be that the meaning is "silver and ornamentation," and when the preposition is removed it becomes accusative.

﴿Or one who is brought up in ornaments﴾: the people of Kufa read *yunashsha'u* with a *damma* on the *ya'*, a *fatha* on the *nun*, and a *shadda* on the *shin*, in the passive voice, meaning "one who is raised by others." Others read *yanshu'u* with a *fatha* on the *ya'*, a *jazm* on the *nun*, and a lightened *shin*, meaning "grows up and becomes great."

﴿In the ornament﴾: in adornment, meaning women. Mujahid said: He permitted women silk and gold, and he recited this verse.

Abdullah ibn Hamid informed us: Muhammad ibn al-Husayn al-Za'farani informed us: Yahya ibn Ja'far ibn Abi Talib related to us: Muhammad ibn Ubayd related to us: Ubaydullah ibn Umar related to us, from Nafi', from Sa'id ibn Abi Hind, from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Gold and silk are forbidden to the males of my community and lawful to its females" [193] [[Fath al-Bari: 10/250; Muntakhab Musnad 'Abd ibn Humayd: 193.]].

﴿And he is not clear in dispute﴾: lacking clarity of argument, due to their weakness and foolishness. Qatada said regarding this verse: A woman seldom speaks with her argument without the argument turning against her. In the Codex of Abdullah (*wa-huwa fi al-kalam ghayr mubin*) [and he is not clear in speech].

Some exegetes said: This verse refers to their idols which they worshipped, honored, and adorned, though they do not speak or utter a sound. Ibn Zayd said: These are their images which they make of silver and gold, and they adorn them and worship them.

This is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas.

Muhammad ibn Na'im informed us: al-Husayn ibn Ayyub informed us: 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-Aziz informed us: al-Qasim ibn Salam informed us: Haytham related to us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he read it *'Ibadu al-Rahman*.

Sa'id said: I said to Ibn 'Abbas: "In my codex it is *'Abd al-Rahman*." He said: "Erase it and write *'Ibad al-Rahman*." The confirmation of this reading is His saying: ﴿Rather, they are honored servants﴾ [[Surah al-Anbiya': 26.]]. The others read *'inda al-Rahman* with a *nun*, and Abu Hatim chose this, saying: Because this is praise, whereas when you say *'Ibad al-Rahman* [servants of the Most Merciful], its confirmation is His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord﴾ [[Surah al-A'raf: 206.]].

﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾: did they attend their creation, so that they would know that they are females? The people of Medina read *ushhidu* in the passive voice, meaning "were they made to witness." *Khalqahum*: at the time they were created. ﴿Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned﴾: that the angels are daughters of Allah.

﴿And they say: "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them"﴾: meaning the angels, according to Qatada, Muqatil, and al-Kalbi. Mujahid said: it means the idols. They are only guessing﴾, meaning lying.

It was said it means blessing. 'Adi ibn Zayd said: "After prosperity, dominion, and blessing (*al-umma*), and We showed them the graves there." It was also said that the two are dialects with one meaning.

*Qal* [he said]: the common reading is in the imperative. Ibn 'Amir read it in the declarative, and Hafs ibn 'Asim related the same.

﴿"Even if I brought you better guidance than that which you found your fathers upon?"﴾: Abu Ja'far read *awa-law ja'akum* with an *alif* [as a question]. The rest read *ji'tukum* in the singular. *Bi-ahda*: with a more correct religion. ﴿They said: "Indeed, we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent." So We took retribution upon them. Then observe how was the end of the deniers.﴾

﴿And [mention] when Abraham said to his father and his people: "Indeed, I am free (*bara'*) from what you worship"﴾: *bara'* means "free"; it is not dualized, pluralized, or feminized, because it is a verbal noun placed in the position of an adjective. In the reading of Abdullah it is *bari'*, with a *ya'*. ﴿Except for He who created me, for He will guide me﴾: created me; the meaning of the verse is: "I am free from every deity except He who created me, for He will guide me to His religion."

﴿And He made it (*wa-ja'alaha*), referring to this statement and word, a word that remains among his descendants﴾: Mujahid and Qatada said: it means *la ilaha illa Allah* [there is no god but Allah]. Al-Qurazi said: it means the will of Abraham that he enjoined upon his sons, which remains in his progeny and offspring, and which Allah mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿And Abraham instructed his sons with it﴾ [[Surah al-Baqarah: 132.]]. Ibn Zayd said: it means his saying: ﴿I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [[Surah al-Baqarah: 131.]], and he recited ﴿He named you "the Muslims"﴾ [[Surah al-Hajj: 78.]].

﴿So that they may return﴾ from their disbelief to obedience, and repent. ﴿But I gave enjoyment to these and their fathers﴾ in this world, so I did not destroy them, nor hasten punishment upon them for their disbelief. ﴿Until there came to them the truth﴾: the Qur'an. Al-Dahhak said: Islam. ﴿And a clear messenger﴾: who clarifies for them the signs and the rulings, and he is Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿And when the truth came to them, the Qur'an, they said: "This is magic, and we disbelieve in it."﴾ ﴿And they said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two towns?"﴾ That is, from one of the two towns. They did not differ that the two towns are Mecca and al-Ta'if, but they differed about who the two men were. Ibn 'Abbas said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira from Mecca, who was called the "basil of Quraysh," and Habib ibn 'Amr ibn 'Umayr al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if.

Mujahid said: 'Utba ibn al-Rabi'a from Mecca, and Ibn 'Abd Yalil al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if. Qatada said: they are al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi and Abu Mas'ud 'Urwa ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi. Al-Suddi said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and Kinana ibn 'Abd 'Amr ibn 'Umayr.

Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Yahya read *ma'ayishahum* [their livelihoods]. ﴿And We raised some of them above others in degrees, that some of them may take others in service (*sukhriyyan*)﴾: that the wealthy may employ the poor laborers with their wealth through work, and that they may use them, so that some become a means of livelihood for others in this world: this one with his wealth, and that one with his work. This is the saying of al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. Qatada and al-Dahhak said: meaning that some own others, so this one is the slave of that one. It was said: some mock others. It was said: some subjugate others.

﴿And the mercy of your Lord﴾: meaning Paradise, ﴿is better than what they accumulate﴾ of wealth in this world. ﴿And if not that the people would become one community﴾: united in disbelief, so they would all become disbelievers. This is the saying of most exegetes. Ibn Zayd said: meaning: ﴿and if not that the people would become one community﴾ in pursuit of the world and preferring it over the Hereafter.

﴿We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful, for their houses, roofs of silver﴾: Abu Ja'far, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Humayd, and Yahya ibn Wathhab read *saqfan* with a *fatha* on the *sin*, in the singular, meaning the plural, by analogy with His saying: ﴿So the roof fell upon them from above them﴾ [[Surah al-Nahl: 26.]]. Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi read *ma'arij*, and both are dialects; the singular is *mi'raj*, like *maftah* and *mafatih*.

"Our glory and splendor have reached the heavens, and we hope for a height beyond that."

That is, an ascent.

﴿And for their houses, doors of silver, and couches of silver upon which they recline, and ornamentation﴾: meaning, We would also have given them, besides that, ornamentation, which is gold, like the phrase "a decorated house." It may be that the meaning is "silver and ornamentation," and when the preposition is removed it becomes accusative.

﴿Or one who is brought up in ornaments﴾: the people of Kufa read *yunashsha'u* with a *damma* on the *ya'*, a *fatha* on the *nun*, and a *shadda* on the *shin*, in the passive voice, meaning "one who is raised by others." Others read *yanshu'u* with a *fatha* on the *ya'*, a *jazm* on the *nun*, and a lightened *shin*, meaning "grows up and becomes great."

﴿In the ornament﴾: in adornment, meaning women. Mujahid said: He permitted women silk and gold, and he recited this verse.

Abdullah ibn Hamid informed us: Muhammad ibn al-Husayn al-Za'farani informed us: Yahya ibn Ja'far ibn Abi Talib related to us: Muhammad ibn Ubayd related to us: Ubaydullah ibn Umar related to us, from Nafi', from Sa'id ibn Abi Hind, from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Gold and silk are forbidden to the males of my community and lawful to its females" [193] [[Fath al-Bari: 10/250; Muntakhab Musnad 'Abd ibn Humayd: 193.]].

﴿And he is not clear in dispute﴾: lacking clarity of argument, due to their weakness and foolishness. Qatada said regarding this verse: A woman seldom speaks with her argument without the argument turning against her. In the Codex of Abdullah (*wa-huwa fi al-kalam ghayr mubin*) [and he is not clear in speech].

Some exegetes said: This verse refers to their idols which they worshipped, honored, and adorned, though they do not speak or utter a sound. Ibn Zayd said: These are their images which they make of silver and gold, and they adorn them and worship them.

This is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas.

Muhammad ibn Na'im informed us: al-Husayn ibn Ayyub informed us: 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-Aziz informed us: al-Qasim ibn Salam informed us: Haytham related to us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he read it *'Ibadu al-Rahman*.

Sa'id said: I said to Ibn 'Abbas: "In my codex it is *'Abd al-Rahman*." He said: "Erase it and write *'Ibad al-Rahman*." The confirmation of this reading is His saying: ﴿Rather, they are honored servants﴾ [[Surah al-Anbiya': 26.]]. The others read *'inda al-Rahman* with a *nun*, and Abu Hatim chose this, saying: Because this is praise, whereas when you say *'Ibad al-Rahman* [servants of the Most Merciful], its confirmation is His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord﴾ [[Surah al-A'raf: 206.]].

﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾: did they attend their creation, so that they would know that they are females? The people of Medina read *ushhidu* in the passive voice, meaning "were they made to witness." *Khalqahum*: at the time they were created. ﴿Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned﴾: that the angels are daughters of Allah.

﴿And they say: "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them"﴾: meaning the angels, according to Qatada, Muqatil, and al-Kalbi. Mujahid said: it means the idols. They are only guessing﴾, meaning lying.

It was said it means blessing. 'Adi ibn Zayd said: "After prosperity, dominion, and blessing (*al-umma*), and We showed them the graves there." It was also said that the two are dialects with one meaning.

*Qal* [he said]: the common reading is in the imperative. Ibn 'Amir read it in the declarative, and Hafs ibn 'Asim related the same.

﴿"Even if I brought you better guidance than that which you found your fathers upon?"﴾: Abu Ja'far read *awa-law ja'akum* with an *alif* [as a question]. The rest read *ji'tukum* in the singular. *Bi-ahda*: with a more correct religion. ﴿They said: "Indeed, we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent." So We took retribution upon them. Then observe how was the end of the deniers.﴾

﴿And [mention] when Abraham said to his father and his people: "Indeed, I am free (*bara'*) from what you worship"﴾: *bara'* means "free"; it is not dualized, pluralized, or feminized, because it is a verbal noun placed in the position of an adjective. In the reading of Abdullah it is *bari'*, with a *ya'*. ﴿Except for He who created me, for He will guide me﴾: created me; the meaning of the verse is: "I am free from every deity except He who created me, for He will guide me to His religion."

﴿And He made it (*wa-ja'alaha*), referring to this statement and word, a word that remains among his descendants﴾: Mujahid and Qatada said: it means *la ilaha illa Allah* [there is no god but Allah]. Al-Qurazi said: it means the will of Abraham that he enjoined upon his sons, which remains in his progeny and offspring, and which Allah mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿And Abraham instructed his sons with it﴾ [[Surah al-Baqarah: 132.]]. Ibn Zayd said: it means his saying: ﴿I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [[Surah al-Baqarah: 131.]], and he recited ﴿He named you "the Muslims"﴾ [[Surah al-Hajj: 78.]].

﴿So that they may return﴾ from their disbelief to obedience, and repent. ﴿But I gave enjoyment to these and their fathers﴾ in this world, so I did not destroy them, nor hasten punishment upon them for their disbelief. ﴿Until there came to them the truth﴾: the Qur'an. Al-Dahhak said: Islam. ﴿And a clear messenger﴾: who clarifies for them the signs and the rulings, and he is Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿And when the truth came to them, the Qur'an, they said: "This is magic, and we disbelieve in it."﴾ ﴿And they said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two towns?"﴾ That is, from one of the two towns. They did not differ that the two towns are Mecca and al-Ta'if, but they differed about who the two men were. Ibn 'Abbas said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira from Mecca, who was called the "basil of Quraysh," and Habib ibn 'Amr ibn 'Umayr al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if.

Mujahid said: 'Utba ibn al-Rabi'a from Mecca, and Ibn 'Abd Yalil al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if. Qatada said: they are al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi and Abu Mas'ud 'Urwa ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi. Al-Suddi said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and Kinana ibn 'Abd 'Amr ibn 'Umayr.

Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Yahya read *ma'ayishahum* [their livelihoods]. ﴿And We raised some of them above others in degrees, that some of them may take others in service (*sukhriyyan*)﴾: that the wealthy may employ the poor laborers with their wealth through work, and that they may use them, so that some become a means of livelihood for others in this world: this one with his wealth, and that one with his work. This is the saying of al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. Qatada and al-Dahhak said: meaning that some own others, so this one is the slave of that one. It was said: some mock others. It was said: some subjugate others.

﴿And the mercy of your Lord﴾: meaning Paradise, ﴿is better than what they accumulate﴾ of wealth in this world. ﴿And if not that the people would become one community﴾: united in disbelief, so they would all become disbelievers. This is the saying of most exegetes. Ibn Zayd said: meaning: ﴿and if not that the people would become one community﴾ in pursuit of the world and preferring it over the Hereafter.

﴿We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful, for their houses, roofs of silver﴾: Abu Ja'far, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Humayd, and Yahya ibn Wathhab read *saqfan* with a *fatha* on the *sin*, in the singular, meaning the plural, by analogy with His saying: ﴿So the roof fell upon them from above them﴾ [[Surah al-Nahl: 26.]]. Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi read *ma'arij*, and both are dialects; the singular is *mi'raj*, like *maftah* and *mafatih*.

"Our glory and splendor have reached the heavens, and we hope for a height beyond that."

That is, an ascent.

﴿And for their houses, doors of silver, and couches of silver upon which they recline, and ornamentation﴾: meaning, We would also have given them, besides that, ornamentation, which is gold, like the phrase "a decorated house." It may be that the meaning is "silver and ornamentation," and when the preposition is removed it becomes accusative.

﴿Or one who is brought up in ornaments﴾: the people of Kufa read *yunashsha'u* with a *damma* on the *ya'*, a *fatha* on the *nun*, and a *shadda* on the *shin*, in the passive voice, meaning "one who is raised by others." Others read *yanshu'u* with a *fatha* on the *ya'*, a *jazm* on the *nun*, and a lightened *shin*, meaning "grows up and becomes great."

﴿In the ornament﴾: in adornment, meaning women. Mujahid said: He permitted women silk and gold, and he recited this verse.

Abdullah ibn Hamid informed us: Muhammad ibn al-Husayn al-Za'farani informed us: Yahya ibn Ja'far ibn Abi Talib related to us: Muhammad ibn Ubayd related to us: Ubaydullah ibn Umar related to us, from Nafi', from Sa'id ibn Abi Hind, from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Gold and silk are forbidden to the males of my community and lawful to its females" [193] [[Fath al-Bari: 10/250; Muntakhab Musnad 'Abd ibn Humayd: 193.]].

﴿And he is not clear in dispute﴾: lacking clarity of argument, due to their weakness and foolishness. Qatada said regarding this verse: A woman seldom speaks with her argument without the argument turning against her. In the Codex of Abdullah (*wa-huwa fi al-kalam ghayr mubin*) [and he is not clear in speech].

Some exegetes said: This verse refers to their idols which they worshipped, honored, and adorned, though they do not speak or utter a sound. Ibn Zayd said: These are their images which they make of silver and gold, and they adorn them and worship them.

This is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas.

Muhammad ibn Na'im informed us: al-Husayn ibn Ayyub informed us: 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-Aziz informed us: al-Qasim ibn Salam informed us: Haytham related to us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he read it *'Ibadu al-Rahman*.

Sa'id said: I said to Ibn 'Abbas: "In my codex it is *'Abd al-Rahman*." He said: "Erase it and write *'Ibad al-Rahman*." The confirmation of this reading is His saying: ﴿Rather, they are honored servants﴾ [[Surah al-Anbiya': 26.]]. The others read *'inda al-Rahman* with a *nun*, and Abu Hatim chose this, saying: Because this is praise, whereas when you say *'Ibad al-Rahman* [servants of the Most Merciful], its confirmation is His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord﴾ [[Surah al-A'raf: 206.]].

﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾: did they attend their creation, so that they would know that they are females? The people of Medina read *ushhidu* in the passive voice, meaning "were they made to witness." *Khalqahum*: at the time they were created. ﴿Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned﴾: that the angels are daughters of Allah.

﴿And they say: "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them"﴾: meaning the angels, according to Qatada, Muqatil, and al-Kalbi. Mujahid said: it means the idols. They are only guessing﴾, meaning lying.

It was said it means blessing. 'Adi ibn Zayd said: "After prosperity, dominion, and blessing (*al-umma*), and We showed them the graves there." It was also said that the two are dialects with one meaning.

*Qal* [he said]: the common reading is in the imperative. Ibn 'Amir read it in the declarative, and Hafs ibn 'Asim related the same.

﴿"Even if I brought you better guidance than that which you found your fathers upon?"﴾: Abu Ja'far read *awa-law ja'akum* with an *alif* [as a question]. The rest read *ji'tukum* in the singular. *Bi-ahda*: with a more correct religion. ﴿They said: "Indeed, we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent." So We took retribution upon them. Then observe how was the end of the deniers.﴾

﴿And [mention] when Abraham said to his father and his people: "Indeed, I am free (*bara'*) from what you worship"﴾: *bara'* means "free"; it is not dualized, pluralized, or feminized, because it is a verbal noun placed in the position of an adjective. In the reading of Abdullah it is *bari'*, with a *ya'*. ﴿Except for He who created me, for He will guide me﴾: created me; the meaning of the verse is: "I am free from every deity except He who created me, for He will guide me to His religion."

﴿And He made it (*wa-ja'alaha*), referring to this statement and word, a word that remains among his descendants﴾: Mujahid and Qatada said: it means *la ilaha illa Allah* [there is no god but Allah]. Al-Qurazi said: it means the will of Abraham that he enjoined upon his sons, which remains in his progeny and offspring, and which Allah mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿And Abraham instructed his sons with it﴾ [[Surah al-Baqarah: 132.]]. Ibn Zayd said: it means his saying: ﴿I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [[Surah al-Baqarah: 131.]], and he recited ﴿He named you "the Muslims"﴾ [[Surah al-Hajj: 78.]].

﴿So that they may return﴾ from their disbelief to obedience, and repent. ﴿But I gave enjoyment to these and their fathers﴾ in this world, so I did not destroy them, nor hasten punishment upon them for their disbelief. ﴿Until there came to them the truth﴾: the Qur'an. Al-Dahhak said: Islam. ﴿And a clear messenger﴾: who clarifies for them the signs and the rulings, and he is Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿And when the truth came to them, the Qur'an, they said: "This is magic, and we disbelieve in it."﴾ ﴿And they said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two towns?"﴾ That is, from one of the two towns. They did not differ that the two towns are Mecca and al-Ta'if, but they differed about who the two men were. Ibn 'Abbas said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira from Mecca, who was called the "basil of Quraysh," and Habib ibn 'Amr ibn 'Umayr al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if.

Mujahid said: 'Utba ibn al-Rabi'a from Mecca, and Ibn 'Abd Yalil al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if. Qatada said: they are al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi and Abu Mas'ud 'Urwa ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi. Al-Suddi said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and Kinana ibn 'Abd 'Amr ibn 'Umayr.

Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Yahya read *ma'ayishahum* [their livelihoods]. ﴿And We raised some of them above others in degrees, that some of them may take others in service (*sukhriyyan*)﴾: that the wealthy may employ the poor laborers with their wealth through work, and that they may use them, so that some become a means of livelihood for others in this world: this one with his wealth, and that one with his work. This is the saying of al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. Qatada and al-Dahhak said: meaning that some own others, so this one is the slave of that one. It was said: some mock others. It was said: some subjugate others.

﴿And the mercy of your Lord﴾: meaning Paradise, ﴿is better than what they accumulate﴾ of wealth in this world. ﴿And if not that the people would become one community﴾: united in disbelief, so they would all become disbelievers. This is the saying of most exegetes. Ibn Zayd said: meaning: ﴿and if not that the people would become one community﴾ in pursuit of the world and preferring it over the Hereafter.

﴿We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful, for their houses, roofs of silver﴾: Abu Ja'far, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Humayd, and Yahya ibn Wathhab read *saqfan* with a *fatha* on the *sin*, in the singular, meaning the plural, by analogy with His saying: ﴿So the roof fell upon them from above them﴾ [[Surah al-Nahl: 26.]]. Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi read *ma'arij*, and both are dialects; the singular is *mi'raj*, like *maftah* and *mafatih*.

"Our glory and splendor have reached the heavens, and we hope for a height beyond that."

That is, an ascent.

﴿And for their houses, doors of silver, and couches of silver upon which they recline, and ornamentation﴾: meaning, We would also have given them, besides that, ornamentation, which is gold, like the phrase "a decorated house." It may be that the meaning is "silver and ornamentation," and when the preposition is removed it becomes accusative.

﴿Or one who is brought up in ornaments﴾: the people of Kufa read *yunashsha'u* with a *damma* on the *ya'*, a *fatha* on the *nun*, and a *shadda* on the *shin*, in the passive voice, meaning "one who is raised by others." Others read *yanshu'u* with a *fatha* on the *ya'*, a *jazm* on the *nun*, and a lightened *shin*, meaning "grows up and becomes great."

﴿In the ornament﴾: in adornment, meaning women. Mujahid said: He permitted women silk and gold, and he recited this verse.

Abdullah ibn Hamid informed us: Muhammad ibn al-Husayn al-Za'farani informed us: Yahya ibn Ja'far ibn Abi Talib related to us: Muhammad ibn Ubayd related to us: Ubaydullah ibn Umar related to us, from Nafi', from Sa'id ibn Abi Hind, from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Gold and silk are forbidden to the males of my community and lawful to its females" [193] [[Fath al-Bari: 10/250; Muntakhab Musnad 'Abd ibn Humayd: 193.]].

﴿And he is not clear in dispute﴾: lacking clarity of argument, due to their weakness and foolishness. Qatada said regarding this verse: A woman seldom speaks with her argument without the argument turning against her. In the Codex of Abdullah (*wa-huwa fi al-kalam ghayr mubin*) [and he is not clear in speech].

Some exegetes said: This verse refers to their idols which they worshipped, honored, and adorned, though they do not speak or utter a sound. Ibn Zayd said: These are their images which they make of silver and gold, and they adorn them and worship them.

This is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas.

Muhammad ibn Na'im informed us: al-Husayn ibn Ayyub informed us: 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-Aziz informed us: al-Qasim ibn Salam informed us: Haytham related to us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he read it *'Ibadu al-Rahman*.

Sa'id said: I said to Ibn 'Abbas: "In my codex it is *'Abd al-Rahman*." He said: "Erase it and write *'Ibad al-Rahman*." The confirmation of this reading is His saying: ﴿Rather, they are honored servants﴾ [[Surah al-Anbiya': 26.]]. The others read *'inda al-Rahman* with a *nun*, and Abu Hatim chose this, saying: Because this is praise, whereas when you say *'Ibad al-Rahman* [servants of the Most Merciful], its confirmation is His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord﴾ [[Surah al-A'raf: 206.]].

﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾: did they attend their creation, so that they would know that they are females? The people of Medina read *ushhidu* in the passive voice, meaning "were they made to witness." *Khalqahum*: at the time they were created. ﴿Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned﴾: that the angels are daughters of Allah.

﴿And they say: "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them"﴾: meaning the angels, according to Qatada, Muqatil, and al-Kalbi. Mujahid said: it means the idols. They are only guessing﴾, meaning lying.

It was said it means blessing. 'Adi ibn Zayd said: "After prosperity, dominion, and blessing (*al-umma*), and We showed them the graves there." It was also said that the two are dialects with one meaning.

*Qal* [he said]: the common reading is in the imperative. Ibn 'Amir read it in the declarative, and Hafs ibn 'Asim related the same.

﴿"Even if I brought you better guidance than that which you found your fathers upon?"﴾: Abu Ja'far read *awa-law ja'akum* with an *alif* [as a question]. The rest read *ji'tukum* in the singular. *Bi-ahda*: with a more correct religion. ﴿They said: "Indeed, we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent." So We took retribution upon them. Then observe how was the end of the deniers.﴾

﴿And [mention] when Abraham said to his father and his people: "Indeed, I am free (*bara'*) from what you worship"﴾: *bara'* means "free"; it is not dualized, pluralized, or feminized, because it is a verbal noun placed in the position of an adjective. In the reading of Abdullah it is *bari'*, with a *ya'*. ﴿Except for He who created me, for He will guide me﴾: created me; the meaning of the verse is: "I am free from every deity except He who created me, for He will guide me to His religion."

﴿And He made it (*wa-ja'alaha*), referring to this statement and word, a word that remains among his descendants﴾: Mujahid and Qatada said: it means *la ilaha illa Allah* [there is no god but Allah]. Al-Qurazi said: it means the will of Abraham that he enjoined upon his sons, which remains in his progeny and offspring, and which Allah mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿And Abraham instructed his sons with it﴾ [[Surah al-Baqarah: 132.]]. Ibn Zayd said: it means his saying: ﴿I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [[Surah al-Baqarah: 131.]], and he recited ﴿He named you "the Muslims"﴾ [[Surah al-Hajj: 78.]].

﴿So that they may return﴾ from their disbelief to obedience, and repent. ﴿But I gave enjoyment to these and their fathers﴾ in this world, so I did not destroy them, nor hasten punishment upon them for their disbelief. ﴿Until there came to them the truth﴾: the Qur'an. Al-Dahhak said: Islam. ﴿And a clear messenger﴾: who clarifies for them the signs and the rulings, and he is Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿And when the truth came to them, the Qur'an, they said: "This is magic, and we disbelieve in it."﴾ ﴿And they said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two towns?"﴾ That is, from one of the two towns. They did not differ that the two towns are Mecca and al-Ta'if, but they differed about who the two men were. Ibn 'Abbas said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira from Mecca, who was called the "basil of Quraysh," and Habib ibn 'Amr ibn 'Umayr al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if.

Mujahid said: 'Utba ibn al-Rabi'a from Mecca, and Ibn 'Abd Yalil al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if. Qatada said: they are al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi and Abu Mas'ud 'Urwa ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi. Al-Suddi said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and Kinana ibn 'Abd 'Amr ibn 'Umayr.

Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Yahya read *ma'ayishahum* [their livelihoods]. ﴿And We raised some of them above others in degrees, that some of them may take others in service (*sukhriyyan*)﴾: that the wealthy may employ the poor laborers with their wealth through work, and that they may use them, so that some become a means of livelihood for others in this world: this one with his wealth, and that one with his work. This is the saying of al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. Qatada and al-Dahhak said: meaning that some own others, so this one is the slave of that one. It was said: some mock others. It was said: some subjugate others.

﴿And the mercy of your Lord﴾: meaning Paradise, ﴿is better than what they accumulate﴾ of wealth in this world. ﴿And if not that the people would become one community﴾: united in disbelief, so they would all become disbelievers. This is the saying of most exegetes. Ibn Zayd said: meaning: ﴿and if not that the people would become one community﴾ in pursuit of the world and preferring it over the Hereafter.

﴿We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful, for their houses, roofs of silver﴾: Abu Ja'far, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Humayd, and Yahya ibn Wathhab read *saqfan* with a *fatha* on the *sin*, in the singular, meaning the plural, by analogy with His saying: ﴿So the roof fell upon them from above them﴾ [[Surah al-Nahl: 26.]]. Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi read *ma'arij*, and both are dialects; the singular is *mi'raj*, like *maftah* and *mafatih*.

"Our glory and splendor have reached the heavens, and we hope for a height beyond that."

That is, an ascent.

﴿And for their houses, doors of silver, and couches of silver upon which they recline, and ornamentation﴾: meaning, We would also have given them, besides that, ornamentation, which is gold, like the phrase "a decorated house." It may be that the meaning is "silver and ornamentation," and when the preposition is removed it becomes accusative.

﴿Or one who is brought up in ornaments﴾: the people of Kufa read *yunashsha'u* with a *damma* on the *ya'*, a *fatha* on the *nun*, and a *shadda* on the *shin*, in the passive voice, meaning "one who is raised by others." Others read *yanshu'u* with a *fatha* on the *ya'*, a *jazm* on the *nun*, and a lightened *shin*, meaning "grows up and becomes great."

﴿In the ornament﴾: in adornment, meaning women. Mujahid said: He permitted women silk and gold, and he recited this verse.

Abdullah ibn Hamid informed us: Muhammad ibn al-Husayn al-Za'farani informed us: Yahya ibn Ja'far ibn Abi Talib related to us: Muhammad ibn Ubayd related to us: Ubaydullah ibn Umar related to us, from Nafi', from Sa'id ibn Abi Hind, from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Gold and silk are forbidden to the males of my community and lawful to its females" [193] [[Fath al-Bari: 10/250; Muntakhab Musnad 'Abd ibn Humayd: 193.]].

﴿And he is not clear in dispute﴾: lacking clarity of argument, due to their weakness and foolishness. Qatada said regarding this verse: A woman seldom speaks with her argument without the argument turning against her. In the Codex of Abdullah (*wa-huwa fi al-kalam ghayr mubin*) [and he is not clear in speech].

Some exegetes said: This verse refers to their idols which they worshipped, honored, and adorned, though they do not speak or utter a sound. Ibn Zayd said: These are their images which they make of silver and gold, and they adorn them and worship them.

This is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas.

Muhammad ibn Na'im informed us: al-Husayn ibn Ayyub informed us: 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-Aziz informed us: al-Qasim ibn Salam informed us: Haytham related to us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he read it *'Ibadu al-Rahman*.

Sa'id said: I said to Ibn 'Abbas: "In my codex it is *'Abd al-Rahman*." He said: "Erase it and write *'Ibad al-Rahman*." The confirmation of this reading is His saying: ﴿Rather, they are honored servants﴾ [[Surah al-Anbiya': 26.]]. The others read *'inda al-Rahman* with a *nun*, and Abu Hatim chose this, saying: Because this is praise, whereas when you say *'Ibad al-Rahman* [servants of the Most Merciful], its confirmation is His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord﴾ [[Surah al-A'raf: 206.]].

﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾: did they attend their creation, so that they would know that they are females? The people of Medina read *ushhidu* in the passive voice, meaning "were they made to witness." *Khalqahum*: at the time they were created. ﴿Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned﴾: that the angels are daughters of Allah.

﴿And they say: "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them"﴾: meaning the angels, according to Qatada, Muqatil, and al-Kalbi. Mujahid said: it means the idols. They are only guessing﴾, meaning lying.

It was said it means blessing. 'Adi ibn Zayd said: "After prosperity, dominion, and blessing (*al-umma*), and We showed them the graves there." It was also said that the two are dialects with one meaning.

*Qal* [he said]: the common reading is in the imperative. Ibn 'Amir read it in the declarative, and Hafs ibn 'Asim related the same.

﴿"Even if I brought you better guidance than that which you found your fathers upon?"﴾: Abu Ja'far read *awa-law ja'akum* with an *alif* [as a question]. The rest read *ji'tukum* in the singular. *Bi-ahda*: with a more correct religion. ﴿They said: "Indeed, we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent." So We took retribution upon them. Then observe how was the end of the deniers.﴾

﴿And [mention] when Abraham said to his father and his people: "Indeed, I am free (*bara'*) from what you worship"﴾: *bara'* means "free"; it is not dualized, pluralized, or feminized, because it is a verbal noun placed in the position of an adjective. In the reading of Abdullah it is *bari'*, with a *ya'*. ﴿Except for He who created me, for He will guide me﴾: created me; the meaning of the verse is: "I am free from every deity except He who created me, for He will guide me to His religion."

﴿And He made it (*wa-ja'alaha*), referring to this statement and word, a word that remains among his descendants﴾: Mujahid and Qatada said: it means *la ilaha illa Allah* [there is no god but Allah]. Al-Qurazi said: it means the will of Abraham that he enjoined upon his sons, which remains in his progeny and offspring, and which Allah mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿And Abraham instructed his sons with it﴾ [[Surah al-Baqarah: 132.]]. Ibn Zayd said: it means his saying: ﴿I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [[Surah al-Baqarah: 131.]], and he recited ﴿He named you "the Muslims"﴾ [[Surah al-Hajj: 78.]].

﴿So that they may return﴾ from their disbelief to obedience, and repent. ﴿But I gave enjoyment to these and their fathers﴾ in this world, so I did not destroy them, nor hasten punishment upon them for their disbelief. ﴿Until there came to them the truth﴾: the Qur'an. Al-Dahhak said: Islam. ﴿And a clear messenger﴾: who clarifies for them the signs and the rulings, and he is Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿And when the truth came to them, the Qur'an, they said: "This is magic, and we disbelieve in it."﴾ ﴿And they said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two towns?"﴾ That is, from one of the two towns. They did not differ that the two towns are Mecca and al-Ta'if, but they differed about who the two men were. Ibn 'Abbas said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira from Mecca, who was called the "basil of Quraysh," and Habib ibn 'Amr ibn 'Umayr al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if.

Mujahid said: 'Utba ibn al-Rabi'a from Mecca, and Ibn 'Abd Yalil al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if. Qatada said: they are al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi and Abu Mas'ud 'Urwa ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi. Al-Suddi said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and Kinana ibn 'Abd 'Amr ibn 'Umayr.

Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Yahya read *ma'ayishahum* [their livelihoods]. ﴿And We raised some of them above others in degrees, that some of them may take others in service (*sukhriyyan*)﴾: that the wealthy may employ the poor laborers with their wealth through work, and that they may use them, so that some become a means of livelihood for others in this world: this one with his wealth, and that one with his work. This is the saying of al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. Qatada and al-Dahhak said: meaning that some own others, so this one is the slave of that one. It was said: some mock others. It was said: some subjugate others.

﴿And the mercy of your Lord﴾: meaning Paradise, ﴿is better than what they accumulate﴾ of wealth in this world. ﴿And if not that the people would become one community﴾: united in disbelief, so they would all become disbelievers. This is the saying of most exegetes. Ibn Zayd said: meaning: ﴿and if not that the people would become one community﴾ in pursuit of the world and preferring it over the Hereafter.

﴿We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful, for their houses, roofs of silver﴾: Abu Ja'far, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Humayd, and Yahya ibn Wathhab read *saqfan* with a *fatha* on the *sin*, in the singular, meaning the plural, by analogy with His saying: ﴿So the roof fell upon them from above them﴾ [[Surah al-Nahl: 26.]]. Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi read *ma'arij*, and both are dialects; the singular is *mi'raj*, like *maftah* and *mafatih*.

"Our glory and splendor have reached the heavens, and we hope for a height beyond that."

That is, an ascent.

﴿And for their houses, doors of silver, and couches of silver upon which they recline, and ornamentation﴾: meaning, We would also have given them, besides that, ornamentation, which is gold, like the phrase "a decorated house." It may be that the meaning is "silver and ornamentation," and when the preposition is removed it becomes accusative.

﴿Or one who is brought up in ornaments﴾: the people of Kufa read *yunashsha'u* with a *damma* on the *ya'*, a *fatha* on the *nun*, and a *shadda* on the *shin*, in the passive voice, meaning "one who is raised by others." Others read *yanshu'u* with a *fatha* on the *ya'*, a *jazm* on the *nun*, and a lightened *shin*, meaning "grows up and becomes great."

﴿In the ornament﴾: in adornment, meaning women. Mujahid said: He permitted women silk and gold, and he recited this verse.

Abdullah ibn Hamid informed us: Muhammad ibn al-Husayn al-Za'farani informed us: Yahya ibn Ja'far ibn Abi Talib related to us: Muhammad ibn Ubayd related to us: Ubaydullah ibn Umar related to us, from Nafi', from Sa'id ibn Abi Hind, from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Gold and silk are forbidden to the males of my community and lawful to its females" [193] [[Fath al-Bari: 10/250; Muntakhab Musnad 'Abd ibn Humayd: 193.]].

﴿And he is not clear in dispute﴾: lacking clarity of argument, due to their weakness and foolishness. Qatada said regarding this verse: A woman seldom speaks with her argument without the argument turning against her. In the Codex of Abdullah (*wa-huwa fi al-kalam ghayr mubin*) [and he is not clear in speech].

Some exegetes said: This verse refers to their idols which they worshipped, honored, and adorned, though they do not speak or utter a sound. Ibn Zayd said: These are their images which they make of silver and gold, and they adorn them and worship them.
